Now, to move it. Dawson grabbed one end of the slab, digging his heels into the sand, and pulled. The rock scraped against the desert floor, grating loudly, but it moved. Slowly, agonizingly, it slid forward.

He repeated the process, inch by excruciating inch, pulling, pushing, adjusting. The sun, now beginning its descent, cast long shadows, but the heat remained intense. His mouth was dry, his muscles screaming, but he pushed on, driven by an almost superhuman will. He was no longer just Dawson, the air ace. He was a beast of burden, a desperate rescuer, a man fighting against impossible odds.

The journey to the truck was a blur of effort and pain. Each time he paused for breath, he would check on Freddy, wiping his brow, whispering encouragement. The sun dipped below the horizon, painting the sky in fiery hues of orange and purple, then giving way to the velvet blackness of night. Still, he pulled.

Hours later, long after darkness had fully enveloped the desert, he finally reached the abandoned truck. He collapsed beside the slab, gasping for breath, his body trembling with exhaustion. He had done it. He had moved Freddy.

He rested for a few minutes, allowing his ragged breath to slowly even out. Then, he forced himself up. He still had work to do.

He pulled the slab, with Freddy still on it, closer to the truck, positioning it so the body of the truck provided the best possible shelter from the wind and, eventually, the sun. He rigged a makeshift canopy from the remaining canvas, stretching it from the truck bed to a couple of sturdy rocks, creating a small, shaded enclosure.

He then set about preparing their camp for the night. He opened one of the canned peaches, forcing himself to eat some, knowing he needed his strength. He sipped the stale water, savoring every drop. He offered some to Freddy, again letting a few drops fall into his mouth, but the young man remained unresponsive.

Dawson sat beside Freddy, watching him, listening to his labored breathing. He felt a deep, profound sense of helplessness. He had done all he could. He had found provisions, moved him to a better shelter. But he was not a doctor. He couldn't fight the fever. He could only wait, and hope, and pray.

He checked the flare gun again, its two cartridges now his last, desperate hope. If he saw anything, any sign of life, he would use them. But what if he used them, and no one came? What if they attracted the wrong kind of attention?

He pulled out the satchel containing the duplicate orders. He still had them. They were safe. But what was the point of delivering them if Freddy didn't survive? The mission, for all its importance, felt hollow, meaningless, without the young man beside him.

He thought of Colonel Welsh again, his stern, unyielding demeanor. He thought of the President, and the terrible blow to the United Nations if their mission failed. The weight of responsibility pressed down on him, heavy and suffocating.

He spent the rest of the night in a grim vigil, dozing fitfully, waking every few minutes to check on Freddy, to wipe his brow with the damp bandana. The fever seemed to ebb and flow, at times appearing to recede, only to surge back with renewed intensity. The desert night was cold, and Dawson covered Freddy with his own jacket, shivering in the chill.

As the first faint streaks of dawn began to paint the eastern sky once more, Dawson felt a renewed sense of urgency. Another day. Another chance. He looked at Freddy. His face was still pale, his breathing still shallow, but there was a flicker, a subtle shift in his expression that Dawson had not seen before. Hope, tenuous and fragile, began to stir within him.

He leaned close to Freddy. “Freddy,” he whispered, his voice raw. “Can you hear me, old man? We’re going to make it. We’re going to deliver these orders. You hear me? We’re going to get home.”

To his astonishment, Freddy’s eyelids fluttered, and for a brief moment, his eyes, though still unfocused, opened. A faint, almost imperceptible murmur escaped his lips.

“Dawson…” he rasped, his voice barely a whisper. “The… the mission…”

Dawson’s heart leaped. He was conscious. Barely, but conscious.

“Yes, Freddy, the mission,” Dawson replied, trying to keep his voice steady. “The mission is still on. We’re going to complete it. Just rest now. Get your strength back.”

Freddy’s eyes closed again, but the faint murmur of his voice, the brief acknowledgment, was enough. It was a sign. A spark of life.

Dawson renewed his efforts, carefully moistening Freddy’s lips, wiping his face. He even managed to get him to swallow a few drops of water. The struggle was far from over, but the darkness of despair had receded, replaced by a glimmer of hope.

He looked out at the vast, desolate landscape, the sun now peeking over the horizon, casting its harsh light across the endless sand. He was still alone, still stranded, still facing impossible odds. But he was no longer fighting for just himself. He was fighting for Freddy, for the mission, for the future.

He took out the flare gun, holding it in his hand, feeling its weight. He knew what he had to do. He couldn't wait any longer. He had to take the risk.

He would climb to the highest point of the abandoned truck, and he would fire one of the flares. It was a gamble, a desperate, last-ditch effort. It might attract enemy patrols. It might attract nothing at all. But he couldn't just sit there and watch Freddy die.

He made his preparations carefully, ensuring Freddy was as comfortable and secure as possible. He replenished their small water supply by pouring the remaining bottle into their canteen. He ate another peach, forcing himself to chew and swallow, needing every calorie, every ounce of strength.

With a deep breath, Dawson climbed onto the roof of the old truck. It groaned under his weight, rusted metal protesting, but held firm. He stood precariously, bracing himself against the wind, his eyes scanning the vast expanse of the desert.

He raised the flare gun, aiming it high into the clear, morning sky. He hesitated for a fraction of a second, his heart pounding in his chest. What if this was a mistake? What if it drew the wrong attention?

But the image of Freddy’s pale, feverish face, the faint, desperate whisper of his voice, cemented his resolve. He had to try.

He squeezed the trigger.

With a sharp *crack*, the flare gun roared, sending a brilliant, red projectile streaking upwards, leaving a trail of smoke against the pale blue sky. It soared, arcing gracefully, then burst open, showering the morning with a cascade of shimmering, scarlet light.

The desert, so vast and silent, seemed to hold its breath. The red light hung in the sky for a long, agonizing moment, a beacon of desperation, a silent plea for help. Then, it slowly faded, leaving only a wisp of smoke and the vast, indifferent emptiness.

Dawson stood there, his arm still raised, his eyes fixed on the spot where the flare had vanished. He waited, straining his ears for any sound, any response. The silence returned, profound and unbroken.

Disappointment, cold and heavy, began to settle over him again. Had it been a wasted effort? A futile gamble?

He lowered the flare gun, his shoulders slumping. He had one flare left. He would save it. For when? He didn't know. Perhaps for when all hope was truly lost.

He was about to climb down when he paused, his head cocked to one side. Was that a sound? A faint, distant drone? Or was it just the wind, playing tricks on his exhausted mind?

He held his breath, straining to hear. The sound, if it was there, was barely perceptible, a low, persistent hum, like a distant swarm of bees. It grew, slowly, steadily, evolving from an indistinct hum into the unmistakable thrum of an aircraft engine.

Dawson’s heart leaped. He spun around, searching the sky, his eyes wide with a sudden, desperate hope.

There! A tiny speck in the far distance, barely visible against the vast canvas of the sky. It was heading their way.

A plane. An actual plane.

He grabbed the remaining flare, his hands fumbling slightly in his excitement. He had to be sure. He had to wait until it was closer, until there was no mistaking its identity.

The drone grew louder, more distinct, the speck in the sky growing larger, resolving itself into a definite shape. It was a twin-engine plane, low-flying, sweeping across the desert like a hawk.

Dawson’s mind raced. Friend or foe? It was the crucial question. He couldn't risk revealing their position to the wrong people.

He peered intently, trying to discern details. The sun was now fully up, and the plane, though still distant, was clear enough to make out its general form. It wasn't German. He was sure of that. The silhouette was wrong.

It was an American C-47 transport plane. The familiar, sturdy workhorse of the Allied forces.

Relief, so overwhelming it almost buckled his knees, washed over him. He wanted to shout, to cry out, but he held it back. He needed to be seen.

He waited until the C-47 was almost directly overhead, its roar now deafening, shaking the very ground beneath him. He raised the flare gun, aimed carefully, and fired his last cartridge.

The red streak shot upwards, directly into the path of the oncoming plane. This time, the pilot would not miss it. He could not.

The C-47 banked sharply, its wings dipping, and began a wide, slow circle. Dawson watched, his heart in his throat, as it descended, circling lower and lower, its reconnaissance now focused solely on their position.

He waved frantically, shouting, though he knew his voice was lost in the roar of the engines. He pointed to the truck, to the makeshift shelter, hoping they would understand.

The plane completed another pass, then circled again, this time much lower. Dawson could make out the faces of the crew in the cockpit, peering down at them. A moment later, a door on the side of the fuselage opened, and something was pushed out. A parachute, small and white, blossomed against the sky, drifting slowly towards them.

It was a supply drop. And, perhaps, a rescue party.

Dawson watched it descend, tears stinging his eyes. They had made it. They had actually made it. Freddy had a chance.

He scrambled down from the truck, rushing towards the landing zone of the parachute. It touched down gently, a canvas bag spilling out its contents. Water, medical supplies, rations, a radio.

He grabbed the radio first, frantically trying to tune it, trying to establish contact. He could hear voices, garbled and distant, but unmistakably human, unmistakably American.

“This is Midnight Raider One,” Dawson shouted into the microphone, his voice hoarse with emotion. “This is Dawson. We have a wounded man. Repeat, wounded man. We need immediate medical evacuation.”

A voice, crisp and professional, responded instantly. “Midnight Raider One, we read you. Loud and clear. Stand by. A ground team is en route. We saw your flare. Hold tight, old man. You’re going home.”

Dawson slumped against the truck, the radio clutched in his hand, relief washing over him in a dizzying wave. He closed his eyes, taking a deep, shuddering breath. It was over. The impossible journey was nearing its end.

He looked at Freddy, lying pale and still, but alive, under the makeshift canopy. He had promised him. He had promised to get him home. And now, by some miracle, by some incredible twist of fate, that promise was about to be fulfilled.

He opened the medical kit, his hands trembling slightly, already planning the immediate care he could provide. He poured fresh water into his canteen, then went back to Freddy, gently washing his face, his neck, his arms. He found sterile bandages, antiseptic. He would do what he could until the ground team arrived.

The waiting was still agonizing, but now it was a waiting infused with hope, not despair. He knew they were coming. He knew help was on its way. The desert, which had been so hostile and indifferent, now seemed to embrace them with a promise of salvation.

As the sun began to climb higher, painting the sky with a new day’s light, Dawson sat by Freddy’s side, watching the distant horizon for any sign of their rescuers. He had faced the impossible, stared death in the face, and emerged, not unscathed, but victorious. The mission, the crucial, world-altering mission, was still intact. And Freddy, his young comrade, his friend, was going to live.

The weight of the world, which had pressed so heavily on his shoulders, had not vanished, but it had shifted. It was no longer a crushing burden of desperate, solitary responsibility, but a shared load, a burden that would soon be lifted. He closed his eyes again, picturing Colonel Welsh’s face, knowing the old colonel would be relieved, perhaps even proud. They had done it. They had done their part. The Midnight Raider, and his loyal companion, had delivered.
